extracted.intended_audience: public administrators, policymakers, political scientists, and reformers interested in designing intelligence/research bureaus for government and industry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating, organizing, and governing intelligence/research bureaus in federal, state, and local government and in industry, including institutional design, staffing, funding, powers, and relationship to decision-makers and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of execution and investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The staff which executes (implements policy) should be separate from the staff which investigates (intelligence/research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two should be parallel but quite distinct bodies: recruited differently, paid if possible from separate funds, responsible to different heads, and intrinsically uninterested in each other's personal success. This avoids investigators becoming administrators who pass down approved decisions and prevents the investigative function from becoming a bureaucracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from Congressional and departmental control
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence officials and bureaus must be independent of the Congressional committees dealing with the department and of the departmental head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence turns mainly on three points: funds, tenure, and access to the facts. If Congress or departmental officials can deprive them of money, dismiss them, or close the files, the staff becomes a creature of those officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable and protected funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Research/intelligence agencies should not depend on annual appropriations that can be manipulated; funding should be entrapped against sly destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed mechanisms include a federal charter creating a trust fund and a sliding scale tied to departmental appropriations to cover minimum overhead and permit growth. The appropriation should be put beyond accidental riders or back-door attacks so that attacks would have to be made openly (e.g., repeal of a charter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional tenure and job security
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenure should provide long-term job security to permit intellectual freedom and continuity in research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend life tenure with provision for retirement on a liberal pension, sabbatical years for advanced study and training, and dismissal only after trial by professional colleagues; conditions similar to any non-profit intellectual career to ensure dignity and freedom of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory access to materials and investigatory powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The bureau should have the legal right to examine all papers, question any official or outsider, and have continuing investigatory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access should be established in the organic act; the bureau should be able to propose accounting methods and, if rejected or violated, appeal under its charter to Congress. Continuous investigation differs from sensational legislative inquiries and fishing expeditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert neutrality and non-advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts must separate their investigative role from advocacy for a particular policy: they must not have a 'policy' in their expert capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experts begin to care too much about particular decisions they will see what they wish to see and cease to represent what they are there to see. The Secretary will distrust experts who appear to be advocating a side; the expert's value lies in representing unseen factors without personal bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actionable, field-applicable reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports must present the elements of the environment so that decision-makers can act as if they were in contact with the field under study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts must translate, simplify, and generalize so the inference applies in the field (e.g., Far East) and not merely on the premises of the report. The goal is to provide to the decision-maker a usable picture, not abstract justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role as accountability link between legislature and department
rubrics_metrics.description: Each intelligence bureau should act as the connecting link between Congress and the Department—'the Congressional eye' on execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the departmental answer to Congressional criticism, permanent visibility of operation may reduce the need for minute legislation born of distrust and thus simplify efficient administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparable standards and measurement across agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt comparable standards of measurement so that records can be exchanged and meaningful comparisons made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If departments use the same measures for the same things (e.g., buying lumber, hiring carpenters), competition and comparisons become possible; standard measures determine the rules and goals of competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quantitative indices and measurement devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Invent and apply index numbers or other quantitative devices for the comparative measurement of social phenomena and administrative performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Index numbers (broadly defined) permit setting up competition between workers, shops, factories, schools, departments, etc. Good indices allow competition to be directed toward desired social goals; examples cited include Ayres' index for state school systems and quota methods used in Liberty Loan campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-agency and regional coordination (federation model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence bureaus at different government levels should federate and coordinate so that comparable accounting avoids duplication and reconciles autonomy with cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional coordination is important where legal frontiers differ from effective environments (e.g., metropolitan health/transportation); coordinated information—rather than centralized decision—allows flexible local autonomy with cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central clearinghouse for assembling problem-specific facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A central agency or clearinghouse should assemble facts tailored to particular decision problems and supply them to the relevant intelligence or diplomatic bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than relying on scattered departmental reports or ad hoc memos, a central clearinghouse would gather and present information in a form suited to the diplomatic or administrative question; could develop into a national-university-like center for research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to scholarship and university linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Information and research functions should be linked to universities: staff recruitment, temporary specialist appointments, student research, and exchange lecturers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except for military and diplomatic secrets, material should be open to scholars; the central agency can become a training ground and supply theses and research problems for political science departments, creating a circulation of talent and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation of staff, data, and criticism to prevent dry rot
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent bureaucratic stagnation by ensuring turnover and exchange of personnel, data, and critical perspectives across government, industry, and universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A circulation of men and data reduces the risks of pedantry, red tape, and insular soft-job cultures; combined with transparency and exchange, it helps keep bureaus effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic incremental implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Intelligence work should be introduced incrementally into existing machinery where openings exist rather than by attempting an all-at-once reorganization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attacking the administrative tangle comprehensively will engage all forces of reaction; the practical way is to begin where feasible, establish footholds, and demonstrate value to build support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against bureaucratic dead weight and inefficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Design institutions to minimize the risk that intelligence bureaus become sources of red tape, useless paperwork, and delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize temptations—soft jobs, pedants, mountains of forms—and counter them by promoting circulation, criticism, comparability, openness, and by focusing on serving decision-makers rather than proliferating paperwork for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical orientation toward decision-makers (not to overburden the public)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary purpose of intelligence bureaus is to aid the man of action—representatives, administrators, and workers—not to require every citizen to digest expert opinion on all matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While useful as a general information source and as a check on the press, the main value is to improve public business by providing expert reporting to those charged with decision and implementation; private citizens will rely on voluntary organizations and experts to digest specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular transparent reporting to create shared factual basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Bureaus should 'hold up a mirror' by regular analysis and reporting so chiefs, subordinates, and the public can see the same facts and reduce obstruction born of mere opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekly or monthly visibility of bureau work, analysis, and comparisons with other bureaus or private corporations moves reform from opinion to measurable fact and makes claims of inefficiency more persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define goals and rules for meaningful competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the goals of competition and the measurement rules so competition serves social aims (efficiency, service), not merely money, power, or popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because competition follows whatever standard is measured, design indices and tests that reflect the social qualities desired—an obscure aim without measurement becomes mere subjective exhortation.
